young.html: François Rabelais was a French monk who became a doctor, and he loved to laugh. He wrote a huge, silly story about a family of giants: Grandgousier, his son Gargantua, and Gargantua's son Pantagruel. The giants are so big that the story can get as wild as Rabelais likes.

Young Gargantua has terrible teachers at first, who make him memorize old books backward and forward. Then a good teacher takes him in hand. He learns by looking at the stars, plants and stones, playing games, making music and talking about what he has read. Rabelais was showing what good learning could be.

Later a hot-headed neighbor king, Picrochole, starts a war over some cakes. Gargantua's kind old father tries everything to make peace. After the war, Gargantua builds an abbey for his friend Friar John, the opposite of a strict monastery, with only one rule.

young.html: For parents: Rabelais is famous for rude, earthy jokes. A good retelling for children, or the chosen chapters on Gargantua's education (Book I, chapters 14 to 24) and the Abbey of Thélème (chapters 52 to 57), suit young readers best.

Design your own abbey. Thélème had six towers, a fountain, libraries in many languages, and a single rule. Draw a plan for a school or clubhouse where people learn because they want to. What is your one rule? Where do you put the library?

full.html: François Rabelais (c. 1494–1553) was a Franciscan and then a Benedictine monk, a student of Greek (a friend by letter of the great humanist scholars), and a doctor who practiced in Lyon. In 1532 he published Pantagruel, and about two years later Gargantua, about Pantagruel's father. Three more books followed, the last printed in 1564 after his death. He wrote in French, inventing words by the hundred.

full.text: Good friends, my Readers, who peruse this Book, Be not offended, whilst on it you look: Denude yourselves of all depraved affection, For it contains no badness, nor infection: 'Tis true that it brings forth to you no birth Of any value, but in point of mirth; Thinking therefore how sorrow might your mind Consume, I could no apter subject find; One inch of joy surmounts of grief a span; Because to laugh is proper to the man.
full.author: Rabelais
full.note: Verse printed as one paragraph. "Proper to" means "belongs to"; a span is about nine inches.

full.html: Under the jokes lies a serious humanist program. Gargantua's first tutors stuff him with rote learning; his new tutor, Ponocrates, fills his day with reading, observing nature, exercise, music and conversation. In Pantagruel, Gargantua writes his son a famous letter urging him to master languages, history, mathematics, law, medicine and Scripture, and warning that "science without conscience" ruins the soul.

When shepherds and cake-sellers quarrel, King Picrochole marches out to conquer the world. Grandgousier, Gargantua's father, offers to pay damages and more, and fights only when he must. Rabelais is mocking wars of conquest and praising rulers who prefer peace, a theme Erasmus also preached.

As a reward, Friar John gets an abbey built to his own design: no walls, no clocks, men and women together, and anyone free to leave and marry. Rabelais describes its six towers, its libraries in Greek, Latin, Hebrew, French, Italian and Spanish, and its gardens. Then he gives its rule.

full.text: All their life was spent not in laws, statutes, or rules, but according to their own free will and pleasure. ... In all their rule and strictest tie of their order there was but this one clause to be observed, Do What Thou Wilt; because men that are free, well-born, well-bred, and conversant in honest companies, have naturally an instinct and spur that prompteth them unto virtuous actions, and withdraws them from vice, which is called honour.
full.author: Rabelais
full.note: Shortened. "Conversant in honest companies" means living among good people.

full.html: Thélème rests on a belief about people: that the well-taught and free, among good companions, will choose good on their own. It is the hope of humanist education. Whether it is wise, naive, or a joke at its own expense is for the reader to decide.
Reading "Do What Thou Wilt" as "do whatever you like, good or bad." Rabelais limits it to people already trained in honor, and his abbey is a picture of what education might make possible.

deep.html: The theologians of the Sorbonne in Paris condemned his books, and Rabelais had to rely on powerful protectors. Some readers have called him a scoffer; others, a reforming Christian humanist who mocked only empty forms. Scholars still argue about his faith, and the books leave room for both views.

deep.text: Laughter as a way of seeing

deep.html: Rabelais mixes high learning with low comedy, lists that run for pages, and words he coins on the spot. The word "Rabelaisian" now means coarse, abundant humor. Later writers from Swift (Gulliver's giants and tiny people, later on this ladder) to the novelists of the 1700s learned from him how much a comic story can carry.

items: Would people really choose good if they were free and well taught, as Thélème assumes?
Why might someone put serious ideas inside a silly story?
Is a war over cakes any sillier than other wars? What is Rabelais saying about pride?

questions: What would a school be like if its only rule were "do what you will"? Would it work for your family?
Gargantua's good teacher used games, music and nature walks. What is the best way you have ever learned something?
Grandgousier tried hard to avoid war. What does it take to keep the peace when someone wants a fight?
Rabelais says laughing is part of being human. What makes something funny, and can a joke be wise?
